Borrowed from Romani ćhaj (“Romani girl, daughter”).

parole.significato: Unruly youth; disobedient child or teenager.
parole.testo: Perhaps from nineteenth-century Romani chavo (“child or youth”). Compare charver, chav.
From Romani chive, chiv, chivvomengro (“knife, dagger, blade”).
Possibly derived from Romani ćor (“thief”), see also Geordie word chor.
Borrowed from Romani koor (“to fight”).

parole.significato: A weapon made of leather-covered metal similar to a blackjack.
parole.testo: Probably from Romani košter (“stick”).
Attested in Britain a. 1570, from Romani kodo (“this one, him”, pronounced /koðo/, ultimately undergoing th-fronting to /kov/ in English), or perhaps directly from Romani kova (“that person”).

parole.significato: A male person, a man; a chap, a chappie.
parole.testo: From cove + -y (diminutive suffix). Cove is derived from Romani kodo (“this one; him”) or kova (“that person”).
From cushty, from Romani kushto, kushti (“good”).
From Romani kushto, kushti (“good”). Perhaps influenced by cushy.
Likely from Romani didikai; compare didicoy.
From Romani dinolo.
Borrowed from Romani gaʒe, plural of gaʒo (“a non-Roma”).
Borrowed from Romani gaʒe, plural of gaʒo. Doublet of gadgie and gorger.
Borrowed from Romani gaʒo. Doublet of gadgie and gorger.

Unknown. Possibly from Etymology 1, via a sense of “a place that will be robbed” in criminal argot; possibly from Etymology 2, via a sense of "cheap theatre"; possibly from Romani gav (“village”) (whence German Kaff (“village”)).
From Romani [Term?].

parole.significato: Mischievous behaviour; dishonest or shady activity.
parole.testo: Possibly a corruption of the Romani expression hakk'ni panki ("great trick", "big con" and hence "shady dealings").

parole.significato: To flirt, to make eyes, to make romantic advances.
parole.testo: Either by analogy with mash (“to press, to soften”), or more likely from Romani masha (“a fascinator, an enticer”), mashdva (“fascination, enticement”). First recorded 1880, and originally mash letter, from mash, masher, likely from Romani masha (“a fascinator, an enticer”), mashdva (“fascination, enticement”), + note. See mash for details.

Either by analogy with masher (“one who presses, softens”), or more likely from Romani masha (“a fascinator, an enticer”), mashdva (“fascination, enticement”). Originally used in theater, and recorded in US in 1870s. Either originally borrowed as masher, from masha, or from mash + -er.
Borrowed from Romani mulo (“dead (man)”).

parole.testo: From Romani patrin (“leaf”), perhaps specifically from an inflected form like Vlax Romani pateryánsa.
Probably from Romani pan (“to stink”).

parole.significato: A Rom; a member of the Romani people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Romani roma, plural of rom (“man, husband, Romani man”). The latter probably comes from Sanskrit डोम्ब (ḍomba, “lower-caste person working as a wandering musician”), from Sanskrit डमरु (ḍamaru, “drum”), which may have been borrowed from a Dravidian language. parole.testo: From Romani romani, feminine form of romano (“of or pertaining to the Roma”), from rom (“man”). See also Roma. Not related to Romanian, Roman or Rome.
From the earlier form rome (“good”, slang); possibly of Romani origin; compare rom.
Origin obscure. Perhaps from shand (“worthless”). Alternatively, perhaps of Romani origin.

From Middle English schaver; equivalent to shave + -er. In its meaning of a boy, lad, recorded since 1592, the word shaver has also been postulated to derive from Romani chavo (“young man”), which also gives us the modern slang chav, ultimately derived from Sanskrit छा (chā, “young animal”).

parole.significato: A smartly dressed person who trades in illicit, black-market or stolen goods, especially during World War II.
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from spiff, spiffy. Spiv was the nickname of Henry Bagster, a Londoner arrested a number of times in 1904-6 for activities as described below, and may have been the archetype. Also possibly from Romani spiv (“sparrow”), as active and opportunistic.
From Romani stariben (“prison”), nominalisation of (a)star (“seize”), causative of ast (“remain”), probably from Sanskrit आतिष्ठति (ātiṣṭhati, “stand or remain by”), from तिष्ठति (tiṣṭhati, “stand”).
From Romani yogger, yogengri (“gun”), from jag (“fire”).
